questions.problem: Let $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $y=2x$ for  $x\in [0,\pi ],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

We start by parametrizing the curve $C.$ A suitable parametrization is

$$
r(t)=⟨t,2t⟩,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$

Then, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ r(\pi ) & =⟨\pi ,2\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(\pi ,2\pi ).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(\pi ))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(\pi ,2\pi )-f(0,0) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi )-(\operatorname{sin}⁡0+\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =(0+1)-(0+1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2}).$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $y={x}^{3}+1$ for $x\in [1,2],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

We start by parametrizing the curve $C.$ A suitable parametrization is

$$
r(t)=⟨t,{t}^{3}+1⟩,\,t\in [1,2].
$$

Then, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨1,2⟩, \\ r(2) & =⟨2,9⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,2)$ and $(2,9).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(2))-f(r(1)) \\  & =f(2,9)-f(1,2) \\  & ={e}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{2})-{e}^{1}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{2}) \\  & ={e}^{2}\cdot 1-{e}^{1}\cdot 0 \\  & ={e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,1⟩ \\ r(4) & =⟨2,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,1)$ and $(2,5).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(4))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(2,5)-f(0,1) \\  & =({2}^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}+2+5)-({0}^{2}\cdot {1}^{2}+0+1) \\  & =107-1 \\  & =106.\end{aligned}

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨1,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(1,3).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

We start by parametrizing the curve $C.$ A suitable parametrization is

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [1,{e}^{2}].
$$

Then, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨1,0⟩, \\ r({e}^{2}) & =⟨{e}^{2},2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,0)$ and $({e}^{2},2).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r({e}^{2}))-f(r(1)) \\  & =f({e}^{2},2)-f(1,0) \\  & =2\cdot {({e}^{2})}^{3}-0\cdot {1}^{3} \\  & =2{e}^{6}-0 \\  & =2{e}^{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
